definition: A substance that produces hydrogen ions (H⁺) when dissolved in water. Has a pH below 7. Examples include hydrochloric acid and sulfuric acid.
A soluble base that produces hydroxide ions (OH⁻) when dissolved in water. Has a pH above 7. Examples include sodium hydroxide and potassium hydroxide.
A substance that neutralises an acid to form a salt and water. Bases include metal oxides, metal hydroxides, and metal carbonates.
The reaction between an acid and a base to form a salt and water. The pH of the resulting solution is closer to 7.
A scale from 0 to 14 used to measure how acidic or alkaline a solution is. pH 7 is neutral, below 7 is acidic, above 7 is alkaline.
A substance that changes colour depending on whether a solution is acidic or alkaline. Universal indicator gives a range of colours across the pH scale.
An ionic compound formed when the hydrogen ions in an acid are replaced by metal ions (or ammonium ions) during a neutralisation reaction.
A strong acid that forms chloride salts when it reacts with metals, metal oxides, hydroxides, or carbonates.
A strong acid that forms sulfate salts when it reacts with metals, metal oxides, hydroxides, or carbonates.
A strong acid that forms nitrate salts when it reacts with bases.
A compound of a metal and oxygen. Metal oxides are bases and react with acids to form a salt and water.
A compound containing a metal, carbon, and oxygen (CO₃²⁻). Reacts with acid to produce a salt, water, and carbon dioxide.
A list of metals arranged in order of their reactivity from most reactive (e.g. potassium) to least reactive (e.g. gold). Used to predict whether reactions will occur.
A reaction where a more reactive metal displaces (pushes out) a less reactive metal from a solution of its salt.
The loss of electrons (or gain of oxygen). In terms of electron transfer: OIL — Oxidation Is Loss.
The gain of electrons (or loss of oxygen). In terms of electron transfer: RIG — Reduction Is Gain.
A reaction in which both oxidation and reduction take place simultaneously. One reactant is oxidised while another is reduced.
A memory aid for redox reactions: Oxidation Is Loss (of electrons), Reduction Is Gain (of electrons).
The breakdown of an ionic compound (when molten or dissolved in water) using electricity. Used to extract metals and to electroplate objects.
An ionic compound in solution or molten state that can conduct electricity and is broken down during electrolysis.
A conductor through which electricity enters or leaves the electrolyte. Consists of a positive electrode (anode) and negative electrode (cathode).
The positive electrode in electrolysis. Negative ions (anions) move towards the anode and are oxidised (lose electrons).
The negative electrode in electrolysis. Positive ions (cations) move towards the cathode and are reduced (gain electrons).
The process of obtaining metals from their ores. Metals above carbon in the reactivity series are extracted by electrolysis; metals below carbon are extracted by reduction with carbon.
An acid that completely ionises in water, releasing all its hydrogen ions. Examples: hydrochloric acid, sulfuric acid, nitric acid.
An acid that only partially ionises in water, releasing only some of its hydrogen ions. Examples: ethanoic acid, citric acid.
A proton produced when an acid dissolves in water. The concentration of H⁺ ions determines how acidic a solution is.
An ion produced when an alkali dissolves in water. The concentration of OH⁻ ions determines how alkaline a solution is.
A reaction in which two solutions are mixed and an insoluble solid (precipitate) forms.
An insoluble solid that forms when two solutions react together.
